question_text: Draw the inductor current waveform in a buck converter with reference to the control signal (the MOSFET gate voltage). Why does it look like that?
answer_text: It is a continuous triangle wave. It ramps up diagonally when the gate is HIGH, and ramps down diagonally when the gate is LOW.
explanation_text: The physics formula is V = L(di/dt). This simply means that applying a flat, constant voltage to an inductor creates a sloped, diagonal current. When the gate is HIGH, a positive flat voltage (V_in - V_out) is applied, creating a straight upward slope. When the gate is LOW, a negative flat voltage (-V_out) is applied, creating a straight downward slope.
bonus_question_text: What dictates how steep that diagonal current line is?
bonus_answer_text: The size of the inductor (L) and the voltage applied. A larger inductor (more Henries) resists change more strongly, resulting in a flatter, less steep slope (meaning less ripple!).
